stem: Who were the Faraizis?
expl: The Faraizis (Faraizi) were followers of the sect run by Haji Shariatullah of Faridpur in Bengal. They advocated many radical religious, social, and political changes. Shariatullah’s son, Dudu Miyan, planned to drive the British out of Bengal. The period from 1818 to 1862 was the main phase of the Faraizi movement; the movement continued even afterward, but its pace slowed down.

stem: Who among the following was the founder of Atmiya Sabha?
expl: To propagate the monotheistic ideals of Hinduism, Raja Rammohan Roy, with the help of his young supporters, founded the “Atmiya Sabha” in 1815. He criticized idol worship and argued with evidence that all ancient original Hindu religious texts preach one Brahman. In support of this, he translated Vedanta texts such as Vedanta Sutra, Vedanta Sara, etc., and also translated five major Upanishads into Bengali.

stem: Raja Rammohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in—
expl: Raja Rammohan Roy founded a new society on 20 August 1828 under the name “Brahmo Sabha,” which later came to be known as the “Brahmo Samaj.” This society opposed idol worship and preached the worship of one Brahman. It was a group of people who believed in the unity of God and stayed away from idol worship. In the Brahmo Samaj, social customs and religious rituals were not given much importance. It emphasized love for all human beings without considering colour, caste, or creed, and stressed service to humanity as the highest way of life. None of the options given is correct.

stem: Who was the founder of ‘Prarthana Samaj’?
expl: The Prarthana Samaj was founded in 1867 in Bombay by Atmaram Pandurang, inspired by Acharya Keshab Chandra Sen. Mahadev Govind Ranade joined this institution in 1868. The main objectives of this institution were: opposition to the caste system, increasing the marriageable age of men and women, promoting widow remarriage, and encouraging women’s education. Ranade’s social reform movement continued successfully till the end of the 19th century.

stem: The best representative of Neo-Hinduism in the second half of the nineteenth century was –
expl: Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission on 1 May 1897 in memory of his guru. After taking sannyasa, he made an extensive study of religious scriptures. The credit for giving a practical form to the interpretation of his guru’s teachings goes to Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902). He described these teachings in simple language. Swami Vivekananda emerged as a propagator of this Neo-Hinduism. In 1893, he went to Chicago, where he delivered his famous speech at the ‘Parliament of the World’s Religions’ (World Parliament of Religions). Through this speech, for the first time, he presented the importance of India’s culture before the Western world in a very effective manner. After this, he travelled in America and England and propagated Hinduism. Swamiji strongly condemned the tendency in Hinduism that says, “Don’t touchism.” According to him, Hinduism had now become confined only to food and drink. He was very unhappy with religion’s silence on the exploitation of the poor by the rich. According to him, to speak of religion to a hungry person is an insult to God and humanity. Vivekananda did not give any political message; yet, through his writings and speeches, he awakened in the new generation a renewed sense of self-respect in their past. He was a true patriot. Subhas Chandra Bose said about him: “As far as Bengal is concerned, we may look upon Vivekananda as the ‘Spiritual Father’ of the modern national movement.”

stem: Dayanand Saraswati founded –
expl: Dayanand Saraswati (Mool Shankar) founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875, whose main objective was to re-establish the ancient Vedic religion in its pure form. The Arya Samaj movement spread mainly as a reaction to Western influences. In 1877, the headquarters of the Arya Samaj was established in Lahore, after which it was propagated more widely. Due to faith in the pure Vedic tradition, Swamiji gave the slogan, “Back to the Vedas.” Swami Dayanand’s objective was to unite India religiously, socially, and nationally. In the religious sphere, he did not accept idol worship, polytheism, avatarism, animal sacrifice, blind faith, tantra-mantra, and false rituals. He considered the Vedas as divine knowledge and accepted literature up to the Upanishadic period. The rules and principles of the Arya Samaj were first framed in Bombay; later, they were edited in Lahore in 1877 and given a definite form. The expansion of Arya Samaj was highly successful in Punjab, and to some extent it also achieved success in Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and Rajasthan. Mahatma Hansraj, Pandit Gurudutt, Lala Lajpat Rai, and Swami Shraddhanand were among its notable workers. In 1893, the Arya Samaj split into two groups—one group supported Western education, while the other opposed it. Among the opponents of Western education, Swami Shraddhanand (another name—Mahatma Munshiram) and Lekhram were prominent. These people founded ‘Gurukul Kangri’ (Gurukul Kangri University) in 1902. Among the supporters of Western education, Lala Lajpat Rai and Hansraj were prominent. These people founded the ‘Dayanand Anglo-Vedic College’.

stem: Who founded the ‘Theosophical Society’?
expl: The Theosophical Society was founded in 1875 in New York by Madame H.P. Blavatsky, a Russian woman (now a resident of Ukraine), American Military Officer Colonel Olcott, William Quan Judge, and others. In 1882, the founders established the Society’s headquarters at Adyar near Madras, which later became its international headquarters. In India, the main objective of this institution was to awaken and strengthen people’s self-confidence in ancient Hinduism and to make religion the main basis of social service.

expl: In 1919, in a jagir of Pratapgarh district, the “Nai–Dhobi Band” was the first instance of an organised act of social boycott. Jhinguri Singh and Durgapal played an important role in it, but soon a new face emerged in the movement—Baba Ramchandra, who not only took charge of the movement but also made it stronger and more combative. Baba Ramchandra belonged to a Brahmin family in Maharashtra. By the middle of 1920, he emerged as a peasant leader and began organising the peasants in Awadh. He had an extraordinary capacity for organisation.

stem: Who demanded the right to enter temples that caused a terrible riot in Tirunelveli in 1899?
expl: On 6 June, 1899, severe riots took place in Tirunelveli (Tamil Nadu). People of the Nadar community had long been demanding the right to worship in temples. When the demand was not met, this riot occurred in the Sivakasi (Virudhunagar district) clash between the Nadar and the Maravar community (Maravan community).

stem: ‘Satyarth Prakash’ was written by –
expl: Mool Shankar (Swami Dayanand Saraswati) was born in 1824 in a Brahmin family in the Morbi princely state (Kathiawar region) of Gujarat. In 1860, in Mathura, he learnt the pure meaning of the Vedas from Swami Virjanand Ji and developed deep faith in the Vedic religion. In 1867, he raised the “Pakhand Khandini Pataka”. In 1875, he founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay. His ideas are described in his famous book “Satyarth Prakash”. His other works include Pakhand Khandan, Rigvedadi Bhashyabhumika, Rigveda Bhashya, Advaitmat Khandan, Panch Mahayagya Vidhi, and Vedaviruddha Matkhandanam.

stem: Who founded the Servants of India Society in 1905?
expl: In the year 1905, Gopal Krishna Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in Poona (Pune). Its objective was to prepare dedicated workers for the service of India and, in a constitutional manner, to promote the true interests of the Indian people. This organisation produced great social workers such as V. Srinivasa Sastri, G.K. Devadhar, N.M. Joshi, and Pandit Hridaynath Kunzru. M.C. Setalvad, B.N. Rau, and Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar were among its prominent members.
